summary: Specifies the Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer (SEAL), which is meant for virtual topologies built by encapsulating packets between border nodes. Such tunnels can introduce failure modes like packet duplication and links with differing Maximum Transmission Units. SEAL is an experimental mechanism for handling these issues.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5320 defines SEAL, a layer that a tunnel can add so that packets still get through when the tunnel's own path is narrower than the path the packet came from. The two ends of the tunnel split and rejoin packets themselves, and they report back to the sender when the path is too narrow, so nothing has to be dropped and discarded to find the right size.

subtitle: A subnetwork layer that carries packets of different sizes through a tunnel without losing them or guessing the path MTU.

tldr.problem: A tunnel adds headers, so packets that fit on the original path no longer fit inside it, and the usual remedies, IPv4 fragmentation and path MTU discovery, both cause serious problems in a tunnel.
tldr.mechanism: SEAL inserts a small header between the inner and outer IP headers. The header carries an extended identification value for duplicate detection and a segment number, so the tunnel endpoints can cut a packet into segments, reassemble them, and report fragmentation back to the source themselves.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document published outside the IETF stream. The protocol number, port and option it uses are taken from the experimental ranges and the memo says they are for experimentation only, not for products.

today: RFC 5320 is an Experimental document from February 2010, published as an independent submission rather than through the IETF stream, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo states that the protocol number, service port and TCP option that SEAL uses are taken from the experimental ranges and are for experimentation purposes only, not to be used in any kind of deployment.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
Many techniques use virtual topologies, including tunnels of one form or another, over an actual network that supports IP. Those virtual topologies have elements that appear as one hop in the virtual topology but are actually multiple IP or sub-IP layer hops, and those hops often have quite diverse properties that are not even visible to the endpoints of the virtual hop.

The memo sets out why the usual answers do not work. IP encapsulation has long been the means for creating such topologies, but the insertion of an outer IP header reduces the effective path MTU as seen by the IP layer. With IPv4 this can be accommodated through IPv4 fragmentation, but unmitigated in-the-network fragmentation has been found to be harmful through operational experience and studies over many years. The IPv4 header Identification field is only 16 bits, so at most 2 to the 16 packets pertaining to the same source, destination, protocol and identification tuple may be active at a given time, and the deployment of high-speed links makes that number too small by several orders of magnitude. IPv4 fragmentation raises issues ranging from slow-path processing in routers to mis-association of the fragments of multiple IP packets during reassembly.

Classical path MTU discovery has its own problems. The source node asks routers in the path to discard the packet and return an ICMP error message when an MTU restriction is encountered, but site border routers are increasingly configured to discard ICMP error messages coming from the outside, in large part because malicious spoofing of error messages is simple since there is no way to authenticate the source of the messages. When a source that needs that feedback does not receive it, a path MTU related black hole occurs, and the source keeps sending packets that are too large.

Tunnels make both problems worse. A site border router acting as a tunnel endpoint may forward packets on behalf of hundreds or thousands of sources; with IPv4 fragmentation that would quickly wrap the 16-bit Identification field and could lead to undetected data corruption, and with classical path MTU discovery the border router may be flooded with ICMP error messages that are untrustworthy or cannot be translated back to the original sources. IPsec tunnels add another problem, because only the first fragment of a fragmented packet carries the transport selectors needed to identify the right security association, which renders fragmentation useless in some cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding a tunnel header makes packets bigger, so they no longer fit on the path inside the tunnel. The two usual fixes both backfire: splitting packets in the network can mix up fragments from different packets, and asking routers to report the size they can handle depends on error messages that many networks now throw away.

sections.title: The Model of Operation
sections.content:
For the purposes of this document, subnetworks are defined as virtual topologies that span connected network regions bounded by encapsulating border nodes. Examples include the global Internet interdomain routing core, Mobile Ad hoc Networks and enterprise networks. Subnetwork border nodes forward unicast and multicast IP packets over the virtual topology across multiple IP or sub-IP layer forwarding hops that may introduce packet duplication or traverse links with diverse Maximum Transmission Units.

SEAL adds a Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer for tunnel-mode operation of IP over subnetworks that connect the Ingress and Egress Tunnel Endpoints of border nodes. Operation in transport mode is also supported when the upper-layer protocols of the border nodes negotiate the use of SEAL during connection establishment. The terms inner, mid-layer and outer refer to the innermost IP layer before any encapsulation, the mid-layer IP after any mid-layer encapsulation, and the outermost IP after SEAL and outer encapsulations.

The SEAL encapsulation introduces an extended Identification field for packet identification and a mid-layer segmentation and reassembly capability that allows simplified cutting and pasting of packets. The SEAL header is inserted between the inner IP and the outer IPv4 headers for simple encapsulations, between the authentication or encryption header and the outer IPv4 headers for tunnel-mode IPsec encapsulations, and immediately after the outer transport layer header for IP encapsulations over transports such as UDP. When it appears immediately after the outer IPv4 header, the SEAL header is processed exactly as IPv6 extension headers are.

SEAL-encapsulated packets carry a 32-bit SEAL_ID, formed from the 16-bit ID Extension field in the SEAL header as the most significant bits and the 16-bit Identification value in the outer IPv4 header as the least significant bits. Routers inside the subnetwork use the SEAL_ID for duplicate packet detection, and the tunnel endpoints use it for SEAL segmentation and reassembly. The memo describes three levels of segmentation: the Ingress Tunnel Endpoint may use IPv4 fragmentation on inner IPv4 packets with the Don't Fragment bit clear before SEAL encapsulation; the SEAL layer itself provides a simple cutting-and-pasting capability for mid-layer packets; and ordinary IPv4 fragmentation is permitted on the outer packet after SEAL encapsulation, used to detect and dampen any in-the-network fragmentation as quickly as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: SEAL is one extra header between the packet and the tunnel's own outer header. It carries a larger identification number, so the tunnel can spot a packet it has already seen, and a segment number, so the tunnel can cut a packet into pieces and put them back together.

sections.title: What the Ingress Tunnel Endpoint Does
sections.content:
The Ingress Tunnel Endpoint configures a tunnel virtual interface over one or more underlying links, and that interface presents a fixed MTU to the inner IP layer as the size for admitting inner packets into the tunnel. The memo explains the reasoning. The nominal Internet cell size has become 1500 bytes, and that is the size end systems have come to expect will be delivered or reported with a suitable message, but the network may not always deliver those messages, so the interface needs a way of conveying 1500 byte or smaller packets to the Egress Tunnel Endpoint without loss and without depending on such messages. The interface MTU should be 1500 bytes plus room for any additional encapsulations that may occur on the path from the original source, while not being so large as to cause a flood of messages from inside the tunnel. IPv6 sources must see a minimum path MTU of 1280 bytes and IPv4 sources should see a minimum of 576 bytes.

For sizing, the endpoint keeps the length of any mid-layer headers and trailers in a variable MHLEN, the length of the outer encapsulating headers in OHLEN, and their sum in HLEN. It keeps a SEAL Maximum Reassembly Unit for each Egress Tunnel Endpoint, initializing it to a value no larger than 2KB, and a SEAL Maximum Segment Size, initialized to the maximum of the underlying IPv4 interface MTU minus OHLEN and the reassembly unit divided by 8.

Inner IPv4 packets with the Don't Fragment bit clear that are larger than the reassembly unit minus the header length are broken up by IPv4 fragmentation. Unfragmentable inner packets that are larger than the maximum of the reassembly unit and the segment size minus the header length are dropped, and an ICMP Packet Too Big or Fragmentation Needed message is sent back to the original source. Each resulting mid-layer packet larger than the segment size is then cut into segments by SEAL itself, at most 8 of them, none larger than the minimum of 1KB and the segment size minus the outer header length. The segments must not overlap, and the endpoint should generate the smallest number of segments possible.

Each segment goes into a SEAL header. For a single segment packet the More Segments bit is 0 and the segment number is 0; for a multi-segment packet the segments carry More Segments 1 and segment numbers 0, 1 and so on, with the final segment setting More Segments 0 and segment number N minus 1. The endpoint then writes the Internet Protocol number of the mid-layer packet into the Next Header field, puts the SEAL protocol number or SEAL port in the outer headers, sets the identification values, and sends the outer packets in canonical order.

To learn the real path size, the endpoint sends probes. Ordinary data packets act as implicit probes, with the Report Fragmentation bit set, so that the other end reports any fragmentation. It also sends explicit probes, with the Acknowledgement Requested bit set, to keep a window of outstanding identification values, which lets it confirm that any ICMP messages it receives are genuine. When it receives a Fragmentation Needed message it lowers the segment size accordingly, and if the message does not carry enough information it searches for a smaller value by sending more packets with the Don't Fragment bit clear, in the same way as classical path MTU discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending end of the tunnel decides how big each packet may be, cuts anything too big into pieces, and numbers the pieces. It also sends occasional probes to find out what the path inside the tunnel really allows, and lowers its own size when the other end reports that the path fragmented something.

sections.title: What the Egress Tunnel Endpoint Does
sections.content:
Egress Tunnel Endpoints must be able to use IPv4-layer reassembly to reassemble SEAL protocol outer IPv4 packets up to 2KB in length, and must also be able to use SEAL-layer reassembly to reassemble mid-layer packets up to 2KB minus the outer header length. The endpoint performs IPv4 reassembly as normal, keeping a conservative high- and low-water mark for the number of outstanding reassemblies pending for each ingress endpoint, discarding incomplete reassemblies when the buffer exceeds the high-water mark, and using a reduced IPv4 maximum segment lifetime value, for example 15 seconds.

When the endpoint processes the first fragment of a SEAL packet that asked for a fragmentation report, it sends a SEAL-encapsulated ICMPv4 Fragmentation Needed message back, with the MTU field set to 0. The message is prepared by encapsulating as much of the first fragment as possible without the length of the message exceeding 576 bytes. The endpoint also sends such a message when a packet asked for an acknowledgement and no fragmentation occurred. When both the acknowledgement and report bits are set and fragmentation occurs, only a single message is sent.

SEAL-layer reassembly is a simple in-order concatenation of the segments of N consecutive SEAL packets from the same mid-layer packet, identified by consecutive identification values. The endpoint keeps recently received segments in a cache for a hold time, using a SEAL maximum segment lifetime of 15 seconds. After reassembly it silently discards the packet if it was a NULL probe, and discards any reassembled mid-layer packet larger than 2KB minus the outer header length that either experienced IPv4 fragmentation or did not arrive as a single SEAL segment. Finally, if the inner packet would cause an ICMPv4 error message to be generated, the endpoint generates a SEAL-encapsulated error message, sends it back to the ingress endpoint, and then accepts or drops the packet according to the type of error. Otherwise it delivers the inner packet to the upper-layer protocol named in the Next Header field.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving end of the tunnel puts the pieces back together, in order, and tells the sending end when the network split something. Error messages travel back inside the tunnel too, so a middlebox filtering them can tell them apart from messages an attacker made up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unlike IPv4 fragmentation, overlapping fragment attacks are not possible, because the requirement is that SEAL segments do not overlap.

An amplification and reflection attack is possible when an attacker sends IPv4 first fragments with spoofed source addresses to an Egress Tunnel Endpoint, resulting in a stream of ICMPv4 Fragmentation Needed messages returned to a victim ingress endpoint. The encapsulated segment of the spoofed first fragment provides the mitigation: the endpoint can use it to detect and discard the spurious messages.

The memo also says the SEAL header is sent in the clear, outside any IPsec or ESP encapsulations, in the same way as the outer headers. As for IPv6 extension headers, the SEAL header is protected only by Layer 2 integrity checks and is not covered by any Layer 3 integrity check.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the segments never overlap, the classic attack of smuggling a second packet inside the fragments of the first does not apply. The header itself is not protected, so it relies on the encryption and integrity of whatever surrounds it.

sections.title: SEAL Against Classical Path MTU Discovery
sections.content:
The memo lists the advantages of the SEAL approach over classical path MTU discovery. Classical path MTU discovery always results in packet loss when an MTU restriction is encountered, whereas with SEAL, IPv4 fragmentation provides a short-term interim mechanism for ensuring that packets are delivered while SEAL adjusts its packet sizing parameters.

Classical path MTU discovery requires routers to generate an ICMP Packet Too Big message for all packets lost due to an MTU restriction, which becomes severe at high data rates and for in-the-network tunnels serving many end systems. Because SEAL ensures that packets no larger than the reassembly unit are delivered, it is enough for the Egress Tunnel Endpoint to return Fragmentation Needed messages subject to rate limiting rather than one for every packet in error.

Classical path MTU discovery may require several iterations of dropping packets and returning messages until an acceptable value is found, whereas under normal circumstances SEAL determines the correct packet sizing parameters in a single iteration. Ordinary packets serve as implicit probes without exposing data to unnecessary loss, and SEAL also provides an explicit probing mode that the classical methods do not have. ETEs encapsulate ICMP error messages in an outer SEAL header, so that packet-filtering middleboxes can distinguish them from raw ICMP messages that may have been generated by an attacker.

The memo calls the most important advantage the fact that all SEAL packets have a 32-bit identification value that can be used for duplicate packet detection and to match ICMP error messages with actual packets sent, without requiring per-packet state. The ingress endpoint can also be configured to accept ICMP feedback only from the legitimate Egress Tunnel Endpoint, which eliminates the packet spoofing denial-of-service attack vectors open to the classical methods.
sections.plainLanguage: Classical discovery works by throwing packets away until you find the size that works. SEAL works by not throwing them away, and by identifying its own packets so that error reports can be matched to them and checked against forgery.

viz.caption: THE PROBLEMS WITH THE USUAL ANSWERS

items.title: The Identification field is 16 bits
items.text: At most 2^16 packets with the same source, destination, protocol and identification may be active at once.

items.title: Fragmentation is harmful
items.text: Issues range from slow-path processing in routers to mis-association of fragments of several packets during reassembly.

items.title: ICMP errors are filtered
items.text: Border routers increasingly discard error messages from outside, and there is no way to authenticate their source.

items.title: Path MTU black holes
items.text: A source that never receives the error keeps sending packets that are too large.

items.title: Tunnels make it worse
items.text: A border router forwarding for many sources can wrap the Identification field or be flooded with error messages.

items.title: IPsec hides the ports
items.text: Only the first fragment carries the transport selectors, so fragmentation can break IPsec.

layers.label: Inner IP packet
layers.detail: The packet being carried across the subnetwork.

layers.label: Mid-layer headers and trailers
layers.detail: Any AH, ESP or other encapsulation between the packet and SEAL.

layers.label: SEAL header
layers.detail: Carries the extended identification and the segment number.

layers.label: Outer headers
layers.detail: The outer IPv4 header and any outer encapsulation.

fields.name: ID Extension
fields.desc: The most significant 16 bits of the 32-bit SEAL_ID value.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Acknowledgement Requested: set to 1 if the ingress endpoint wants an explicit acknowledgement.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Report Fragmentation: set to 1 if a report is wanted if any IPv4 fragmentation occurs.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: More Segments: set to 1 if this packet holds a non-final segment.

fields.name: RSV
fields.desc: Reserved for future use; must be set to 0.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: An Internet Protocol number, as for the IPv4 protocol and IPv6 next header fields.
